subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
subsubtopic: NIGERIA AND DISCUSSIONS WITH U THANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to report on certain initiatives taken within the last few days by the Canadian government in the international field.

Some two weeks ago discussions commenced in my office and in the Department of External Affairs about the desirability of sending to Lagos a personal representative of the Prime Minister of Canada for the purpose of furthering Canadian assistance efforts to that country. As a result of the decision reached in those discussions I instructed Mr. Ivan Head, my legislative assistant, to travel to Nigeria to speak on my behalf to Major General Yakubu Gowon, the head of the Nigerian federal military government.
Mr. Head left Canada on Saturday, October 26. He met with General Gowon in Lagos on Tuesday of last week. They talked at some length with respect to the unfortunate hostilities now raging in Nigeria. On my behalf Mr. Head expressed to General Gowon the deep sympathy of all Canadians for the people's suffering as a result of the civil war. These sentiments were understood and welcomed by General Gowon. Discussed as well was the means by which the desire of Canadians to assist in the alleviation of that suffering could be made more effective.
As an immediate result of the Lagos talks, I am happy to be able to report the following. First, General Gowon has agreed to assist in every way possible and to guarantee the safety of daylight Red Cross flights into Uli airstrip from either or both of Lagos and Fernando Po. This means that the daily volume of relief supplies which could be carried into the rebel area could be multiplied several fold. This statement by General Gowon is, I suggest, both significant and laudatory. It illustrates clearly the sincerity of the federal military government in its declarations of good faith toward the Ibo peoples.
General Gowon has placed a single condition on this guarantee, one which I regard and which I am sure all Canadians will regard as eminently reasonable. It is that Colonel Ojuk-wu will undertake not to employ the Uli airstrip during daylight hours for arms flights. In this regard it should be borne in mind that such an undertaking would in no respect reduce the present level of arms shipments to the rebels. Uli airstrip is not now being used for any purpose during daylight hours. Under the agreement now reached it would be used, but only for civilian relief purposes.
I therefore now address a public and urgent appeal to Colonel Ojukwu to seize this opportunity to open up his airport to daylight relief flights and so permit the Red Cross to increase substantially food shipments to those civilians in the rebel held areas needing help.
A second point emerging from the Lagos talks was the useful information exchanged with respect to the most effective form of assistance which Canada might offer to Nigeria respecting distribution of relief supplies in federal territory. These discussions are continuing at an official level and I hope to be able to make a further announcement in this respect at an early date.
Third, the talks proved useful as an occasion for discussing Canada's participation in the international observer team. General Gowon repeated his assurances that the team will continue to enjoy freedom of movement and access.
I should like to report as well, Mr. Speaker, that on Saturday afternoon I met in New York with His Excellency U Thant, the Secretary General of the United Nations. We

Statement Respecting Nigeria employed that opportunity to exchange views on a number of issues of interest to Canada and to the United Nations. This was the second occasion since assuming the office of Prime Minister that I have engaged in lengthy and useful talks with the Secretary General, the first being in Edmonton in May. We have agreed to continue this practice from time to time.

I draw these recent activities to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, as an indication of the continuing initiatives of the government to ensure that Canadian foreign policies are both effective and appropriate.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
subsubtopic: NIGERIA AND DISCUSSIONS WITH U THANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement of the Prime Minister will be received with pleasure, I am sure, by all those who have felt that the government was somewhat slow in initiating an imaginative policy in so far as the humanitarian and political aspects of the Nigeria-Biafra war are concerned. As one who has been following some of the concepts of the Prime Minister's office about communications and the need to improve them, I am interested to see how this example of public attitude to foreign affairs has somewhat surprised the Prime Minister and his government in that they have found they cannot turn the public on and off like a tap. This they tried to do in the case of Nigeria and Biafra.
Certainly I welcome the initiative that the government has at least taken in sending one of its emissary, a senior person in the Prime Minister's office, to Lagos. I hope the gentleman concerned took the opportunity to make his appeal while he was in West Africa, not only to General Gowon but also to Colonel Ojukwu. Perhaps this would have avoided the necessity of the appeal of the Prime Minister. I think this very satisfactory, since the observer team, which has been under some rather restrictive prohibitions, about which it commented in its report; and has been guaranteed freedom of movement and access by the government of Nigeria. It will be a useful change if the observer team is enlarged and is also able to visit Biafra.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
subsubtopic: NIGERIA AND DISCUSSIONS WITH U THANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure every member of this house who represents the Canadian people is happy to see that the deep concern of the Canadian public in relation to the situation in Biafra is reflected in the statement the Prime Minister has made. It was quite a long statement covering a number of complex matters.

DEBATES	November 4, 1968
I would simply welcome the proposal that daylight flights are to be made, perhaps thereby enabling the delivery of needed food and medical supplies to be doubled.
However, Mr. Speaker, I note once again that the Prime Minister referred to Lagos and Fernando Po. May I remind the Prime Minister that there is another highly successful operation going on, one that has been going on for several months, from Sao Tome.
I appreciate there is difficulty here unless the operation is also carried out under the International Red Cross. If instead of ignoring that operation the government of Canada were to do its best to see that the Red Cross and the churches entered into an arrangement satisfactory to the Nigerian government for the inspection of flights from Sao Tome, then I suggest supplies would not only be doubled but quadrupled, or perhaps even better.
I am glad the question of the observer team was taken up but I did not notice in the Prime Minister's statement any sort of undertaking by the Nigerian government that they would change the terms of reference. I remind the Prime Minister that it was made absolutely clear in the report of the observers that the future efficacy of the operation depended upon there being some change in the terms of reference.
I also suggest that their future efficacy depends on their having an opportunity to go into the Biafran occupied areas in order to hear complaints that may be made. This would make the observer team infinitely more useful than it is now.
I must say that I still regret in this statement, much though we welcome it, the complete absence of any reference to the overriding necessity of bringing about a cease fire and stopping the importation of arms by either side in the conflict. It seems to me this is something which in the interests of humanity and under the rules of international law cannot be disregarded by the international community. We shall continue to express our regrets until Canada takes the lead we think she could take in this respect.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING
subsubtopic: NIGERIA AND DISCUSSIONS WITH U THANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me on behalf of the Rallie-ment Creditiste, to congratulate most sincerely the right hon. Prime Minister for his initiative in helping the people of Biafra, who seem to be threatened by inevitable suicide because the federal troops have tried to keep the province from obtaining its liberty.
November 4, 1968

We, on this side of the house, are always too pleased to support legislation or any government initiative to help a people in need. But, if poor legislation or an unacceptable project is introduced, we will be equally pleased to expose our views.
I congratulate you, Mr. Prime Minister, on that government initiative which will be appreciated by all the countries of the world. However, I am sorry that 34 days were needed to take the initiative-which I myself requested 34 days ago-especially if we take into account the fact that 6,000 people were dying every day and that the government could have avoided a great number of killings by acting sooner.
Mr. Prime Minister, your work is only starting, since this morning we read in the newspapers that 200 Nigerians had been killed. Furthermore, a press release from the Biafran army indicates that the battle was fierce, that an impressive number of soldiers were killed and that the Biafrans also seized hundreds of English-made rifles and a substantial quantity of ammunition.
If a country such as Great Britain, supported by Canada, on the one hand, can pretend to render service to these people while, on the other hand, it ships arms, I say that this is mass-killing, and therefore, Mr. Prime Minister, you are fully responsible for rescuing a province which wanted to protect its oil wells.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is a fact that his government has resurrected the proposal which was turned down by the provinces several years ago, to offer an additional 17 points of personal income tax to those provinces which would take over the hospital plan, the Canada assistance plan and the program of health care; and would the Prime Minister say whether this is the only proposal of substance, rather than of detail, which the government of Canada has made to the federal-provincial conference of finance ministers?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I do not want to comment in too great detail on these talks which are beginning today and which will continue tomorrow. The Minister of Finance will be here to reveal any part of the discussions on which there is agreement, or agreement to disclose; but in a general way I can say that the government of Canada has renewed, with slight modifications, the offers which were made in the fall of 1966.
DEBATES	November 4, 1968

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: As a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, arising out of the reported remarks of Prime Minister Bertrand this morning concerning the 2 per cent social development surcharge and the remarks of the provincial treasurer of Ontario concerning the futility of the federal-provincial conference as a result of the timing of the budget, will the Prime Minister say whether the 2 per cent surcharge in particular is subject to any review by the government?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, because we think it is erroneous on the part of the provinces to submit that this 2 per cent tax is linked specifically to medicare, as they do in their briefs. It is a general tax for social development purposes, and has been imposed to meet the escalation of costs in many areas of expenditure.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister advise the house whether this renewed offer of 17 points on the income tax bears the characteristics of the previous offer, that these would be subject to refunds from the provinces if the yields in this field of taxation were in excess of the costs of the programs for which they were being turned over to the provinces?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the offer made in 1966 was perhaps slightly different from that which I understand the hon. member to be saying. It was 17 per cent as a transfer of fiscal points plus a supplementary to equalize total receipts, so it would cover the expenditures which are variable. Seventeen per cent did not mean the same thing for all provinces because of the differences in size and so on. It was 17 per cent plus a supplementary amount which was meant as an equalization amount.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister say whether his government is making specific proposals to the provinces, either at the finance minister' meeting or at the meeting of the minister of health, with regard to a ceiling or some other formula for the control of the shared cost programs? maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
During the discussions there will arise certain suggestions on our part as to ways in which expenditures might be limited, but we are making them only by way of suggestions. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, the expenditures themselves are

November 4, 1968

controlled by the provinces and we are not in a position to force them or to suggest that they do anything in particular that they do not want to do themselves. We are exploring with them certain ways in which savings might be achieved if they so desire.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: The government of Canada is not proposing any specific ceiling for these expenditures to the provinces, nor any departure from the existing agreements except such new agreements as may be reached with the approval of the provinces?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Generally speaking that is correct, Mr. Speaker. We are not proposing any unilateral cessation of agreements which have been reached by both parties at the present time. We are suggesting that they either be phased out, if we have the right to phase them out, or that they be allowed to expire in certain cases and perhaps not renewed. We are taking the position that both parties together should look now for a decrease in expenditures before any renewal period or expiration period is reached.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In other words we, the federal government, are raising taxes now and giving the produce to the provinces. After five years when the program
Inquiries of the Ministry is well established we suggest that the provinces raise the taxes themselves, and the federal government will evacuate that tax room to an equivalent amount.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext: Perhaps I should not have asked the question.

speechtext: Is the just society of five years' duration?

speechtext: Since the federal government is to vacate its responsibility for financing medicare at the end of five years, is it also the intention of the government of Canada to vacate the social insurance plan on its own if this is legally possible under existing agreements?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS PROPOSED TRANSFER TO PROVINCES OF FISCAL POINTS IN RELATION TO SHARED COST PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member over there is showing his ignorance, but there is nothing new about that. The five years is not something I have invented today. It is something which has been set out in the law and which was discussed with the provinces at the time medicare was being set up. So there is nothing surprising about it.
On the point raised by the Leader of the Opposition, I might say in a general way that we indicated in 1966 and repeat now that it is our intention to get out of a lot of these areas of social services and let the provinces assume them. We will give them the tax room which goes along with these expenditures. We decided in 1966, and are following the policy now, to have all the provinces follow the precedent set with regard to the province of Quebec, whereby that province has much more tax room than the other provinces but also has much greater responsibility for the spending. This is nothing new. It was announced a full two years ago.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Defence Production):
speechtext:
The estimates which we are considering today, Mr. Chairman, reflect

DEBATES	November 4, 1968
the changes that have either been undertaken in the new department of supply and services or those which are contemplated in the immediate future. In introducing these estimates there are just a few comments I should like to make so new members in particular may be better informed on just how this department functioned in the past.
Quite frankly, since this is my first responsibility in this regard it will give me an opportunity as well to set the picture, as it were, in proper perspective. The Department of Defence Production, as you know, has been in existence since 1951. The primary purpose of the department up to now has been to act as the procurement agency for the Department of National Defence. I believe it was generally agreed, and I think the record has tended to support this assessment, that it was in the best interests of public expenditures and of the nation generally to have a civilian oriented department undertake the job of procurement of the many and varied needs of the Department of National Defence. More recently, as a result of the general recommendations of the Glassco commission and since approximately 1963 or thereabouts, additional responsibilities have been assigned to the Department of Defence Production giving it the responsibility for purchasing on behalf of a number of civilian departments. Members will be interested to know that to date the amount of work in this connection that has been done embraces between 35 and 40 civilian departments or agencies. We are now responsible, in the department, for approximately 60 per cent of the expenditures on purchases by civilian departments.
As the transition continues and transfer of this purchasing authority continues to be brought over into our area of responsibility, it is expected that we will, within a comparatively short time, reach a point where we are doing a very substantial amount of, if not all, the purchasing for civilian departments. I think the record of the department is an indication that the concept of combined buying is equally as defensible and effective as has been the concept of a civilian department buying for the armed forces. We are planning now to continue to extend this consolidation and, as members will know, in July of this year it was announced that we are to establish a new department of supply and services.
Very briefly, this department will embrace those activities which I have already outlined to members, that is, purchasing for the armed
November 4, 1968

forces and a continuation of purchasing on behalf of civilian organizations. It will embrace these and a number of other very important functions. On the supply side, the department of supply and services is tp undertake the major portion of what were, up to now, the shipbuilding responsibilities of the Department of Transport. In this way we will assume most of the things which the Department of Transport has been doing for itself in terms of design, procurement, the issuance of contracts and the general followup operations on shipbuilding projects to meet D.O.T.'s needs.
It is intended also that there will be an extension of the responsibilities which up to now have belonged to the Department of Defence Production with regard to the Queen's printer and the Canadian government printing bureau.
On the services side of the new department, and the estimates are presented in such a way that hon. members will have an opportunity to deal with both supply and services functions more or less simultaneously, the central element that will be brought over into the new department will be the comptroller of the treasury which up to now has been the responsibility of the Department of Finance. As you know, the comptroller of the treasury has a great many important responsibilities. These include, of course, the duty and function which, I suppose if one wished to oversimplify, could be called bookkeeper to the Canadian government. There are a variety of other services that are performed by the comptroller of the treasury, and some of these and the extension of them that we propose I will deal with in just a moment.
The second function which is to be assumed by my new department will be responsibility for the central data process service bureau. A third responsibility will be for the bureau of management and consulting services. If members will permit me, I should like to spend a few moments outlining the specific ideas that we have and the specific responsibilities which will be exercised under these headings.
The central data process service bureau is a reflection of an important change which is evident not only in government but in industry, with regard to the greater use of computers and other data processing equipment of one kind or another. The establishment of this bureau would mean that we would employ these new techniques in the best and
Supply-Supply and Services most efficient way possible. I want to emphasize that it is not intended we will create a single unit that will do all the data processing for all departments of government. There will be specific responsibilities and specific jobs each department will continue to do for itself, but by and large the objective is to establish a new, central data process bureau as a facility which will be available to all departments that require it. In addition, we will thereby build up a bank of experts on computers and the like so all departments will have the capacity to draw on these and gain the benefits of the experience and knowledge these authorities possess.
The bureau of management and consulting services is, I think, also a most useful part of government structure. It is one which I believe will be employed more and more in the future. Essentially, the function of this bureau is to provide for any government department or agency expert advice to review procedures within a given department, to analyse the techniques that are being employed and to make recommendations or provide other help which will enable these departments to perform in a more efficient manner.
The department has achieved quite an impressive record in the past year. There have been some 60-odd studies which have been made at the request of specific departments and the results of these have, generally speaking, been very productive. They have brought about improvements in the functioning of these departments and agencies.
Returning for a moment, if I may, to some of the responsibilities on the supply side of the department of supply and services, I have outlined what its functions are. In this current year we have a number of special projects, most of which I believe are listed in the estimates. There are one or two, however, to which I should like to call particular attention as they represent some of the major areas for which we are now responsible in the defence production field. There is, for example, a construction program for the CF-5 aircraft centred in Montreal but with benefits in other regions as well. Under this program we are the responsible agency for the contract which will result in the construction of 115 of these CF-5 aircraft. There is at the same time, within the production facility where these are being built a similar order, not necessarily in size but for that type of aircraft, for the government of the Netherlands. These two
2370	COMMONS
Supply-Supply and Services projects are going forward simultaneously. My main reason for mentioning the Netherlands order is to give an indication of the international co-operation which my department, in co-operation with others, has been able to achieve and which I believe has resulted in very substantial benefits not only in terms of government orders but in terms of our assistance to Canadian industry, particularly industry that is oriented to the defence field.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The second major project that is now under way and in which hon. members will be interested concerns the contracts already issued for the construction of D.D.H. destroyers. I confess that I have had a great deal of trouble within my department trying to keep all the initials correct, but I think I am right in saying that this is the official designation at the moment of these four vessels. Two of them are being built at Sorel in Quebec and two at Lauzon in Quebec. This is probably the single major defence construction project under way at the present time.
In addition to the shipbuilding work on these four vessels there is an enormous amount of what I choose to call complementary work, that is to say, work on the various equipment needs of these vessels, and these items are being constructed and designed in many different parts of Canada. If hon. members so desire I would be pleased to outline where these contracts have been placed and their nature.
In addition to these two major projects, as I describe them, the Department of Defence Production is also very directly engaged in a number of other projects of a defence nature. It has, as well, been participating in a number of international programs which have resulted either through direct involvement by government, or, in an indirect way, through the initiatives that we have taken, in considerable foreign sales of one kind or another. I have mentioned the Netherlands air force as one example. Another is that just recently some 15 of our Buffalo aircraft which originated as the result of a D.N.D. requirement have been sold in South America.
In addition to the new construction of the magnitude I have outlined, Mr. Chairman, there is a continuing repair and overhaul requirement. This amounts to many millions of dollars annually. It is one of the more difficult areas, as some hon. members will know, because of the need to try at least to

DEBATES	November 4, 1968
ensure that most of the facilities in Canada do have a capability in this regard. We try to see that each gets a portion of this work.
This is not always easy, Mr. Chairman. Indeed, I would go so far as to say that it is extremely difficult to bring into line, to rationalize, if you like, the needs of individual plants with the other and fundamental requirement which I suggest rests on my department, namely, that of getting the best value possible for our defence dollars, as well as for our purchasing dollar generally.
Our total purchasing in the department in the current year is in excess of $1 billion. This is a very sizeable sum of public money and I am deeply conscious of the responsibilities that are ours in ensuring, as I said, that our money is spent to best advantage. Of this $1 billion plus, about $500 million or slightly more than half that amount is for the Department of National Defence. These are direct and specific requirements of the Department of National Defence and we, as the procurement agency, follow through on their demands. In addition to these expenditures on behalf of the Department of National Defence, the remainder, or about 45 per cent, of the expenditures are included under a general heading: for example, purchases on behalf of foreign governments in Canada as a result of various international agreements of one type or another.
We have also undertaken some expenditures on behalf of external aid programs when it has appeared that the use of the expertise that we possess has been desirable in order to obtain the best kind of arrangement. This is not, I should add, a total involvement on our part. It is not one of the agencies that has been completely transferred to the Department of Defence Production in terms of its purchasing needs. Where we have demonstrated or it is obvious that we can be of assistance, we have made certain external aid purchases.
Then there is the money that is spent on behalf of civilian or civil departments. When the total transfer of these civil departments is completed, which I anticipate will be over the next year to two years, we will then be adding to the total procurement value for which my department is responsible an extra $100 million, or an amount in that neighbourhood. That is our general assessment.
There are some interesting statistics in relation to the service side of the department in which I think hon. members may be interested. As most hon. members know, we
November 4, 1968	COMMONS
are the cheque issuing agency for the federal government. All payments go through the comptroller of the treasury. In the present year the government will issue in the neighbourhood of 78.5 million cheques. This number of cheques will go out from various government agencies and departments.
It is also interesting to note that of this total of 78.5 million cheques, about 53.5 million are taken care of under about three headings. These include, for example, family allowance payments, old age security, family assistance and the like. So in total 78.5 million cheques are issued, with 53.5 million of these cheques being issued under various social programs.
I should also add that in the consultation process in which we are engaged, which was going on long before I was responsible for the department and is now being accelerated in view of our intentions in this matter, we have in operation the central travel service which, from all accounts and from what I have been able to determine in my short time in the department, is a very useful and productive new operation. This is the centralization of all travel requirements and various related needs of government departments, and it is working out extremely well.
We have also introduced the vehicle fleet management information service. Related to this-and I suspect this will interest hon. members-we have in this year undertaken a consolidated vehicle purchase program. This means that we will adopt a sort of master contract approach which gives us the chance to take the best advantage of our purchases in terms of price, quality and the like. With the exception of external affairs, where there are a variety of unique problems inasmuch as vehicles are being exported overseas and we have not yet ironed out all the technicalities, we are now purchasing all the vehicles for civilian departments.
I believe this represents in capsule form some of the developments that are under way. The only other matter to which I should like to refer specifically concerns the Department of Public Printing and Stationery. As hon. members know-and I suppose this is the most familiar of all its activities-the Canadian government printing bureau is responsible for the publication of statutes and for the preparation and publication of the myriad documents-indeed, I am sure hon. members sometimes feel there are far too many-which are required in connection with

Supply-Supply and Services the House of Commons and the general activities of government.
In addition, the Queen's printer has a special responsibility in terms of acting as adviser and the giving of expert assistance with regard to the best, most efficient and least costly way of preparing various government documents and the like. Perhaps hon. members will be interested to learn that in the run of a year through the printing bureau and the Queen's printer we produce-the figure will vary, of course, from one year to the next-several thousand documents. I was going to call your special attention, Mr. Chairman, to the increase during centennial year when, as you know, a number of very special books and the like were produced which gained international recognition. Indeed, in one case the book, "The Year of the Land," won an international award as well.
The result of this kind of activity-it was mainly attributable to centennial year-was an increase last year of 47 per cent in the sale of various documents, of the total available output of the Queen's printer, if you wish. Normally the increase in sales is approximately 10 per cent annually.
We have also been going through the process of providing outlets in at least each one of the major regions of Canada. In these centres we have a sales facility so that interested parties can obtain any government document in which they are interested. By and large these book stores have been very successful and have provided what appears from all the evidence that reaches us a most worthwhile service.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Before I conclude what I was going to say there is one other point that I should mention in connection with the supply side. Another of our assignments is to consolidate the purchasing and the warehousing of the needs and supplies of the department. This is the commodity approach to purchasing. We now have a pilot plant under study in the capital region under which we will bring together the known needs of a common nature of all departments and supply those departments directly from this type of centralized warehouse. This pilot project has only advanced to perhaps 10 per cent of its ultimate effectiveness but already we are satisfied that it represents real savings. For example, the best assessment I obtained as of today is that in the capital region, adopting this commodity approach and the centralized warehousing
November 4, 1968

Supply-Supply and Services idea, our savings will probably be approximately $3 million annually. We suspect, on the basis of what is known so far, that we can look for savings of 10 per cent to 20 per cent over all in our purchasing requirements generally when this system is fully functional.
I believe that is as much as I can tell hon. members at the moment about the background of the department and the plans we have. All this is, I think, evidence that we are moving in a most complex and difficult field to bring the most modern management and control techniques available to the service of government. When the job is finished we hope to have a very substantial pool of experience and expertise, as I have described it, available to all departments. We hope to remove from those departments responsibilities which more properly can be undertaken by a more central agency, which will leave them free to pursue their main assignments and responsibilities.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to note the ready grasp the minister has of his department and its objectives. Obviously the minister has had experience in operating concern of substance. He is capable of running this department efficiently and in a manner that will truly benefit the taxpayers of this nation.
The minister touched on most of the Glas-sco commission's recommendations and I am pleased to note that substantial savings have already been made as a result of the central warehousing pilot plant that has been established in this area. This indicates how great the benefits to the taxpayers will be if all those suggestions are implemented on a national basis.
I am also pleased to note that in many areas manpower is to be cut down, as recommended by the Glassco commission. Those who are concerned about the proliferation of jobs in our public service will be especially pleased with this. I assure the minister that he will receive every consideration from the official opposition in his endeavours to eliminate red tape and streamline and modernize the government's purchasing program.
Since I represent a constituency containing an aircraft plant I am probably more closely associated with that part of the former department of defence production having to do with aircraft matters than with other parts of the department which have fallen under the minister's responsibilities. In dealing with officials of the department on matters pertaining to the government's aircraft program I

have become aware of their keen awareness and helpfulness and their desire to do everything humanly possible to facilitate the wellbeing of industries that are located in the Atlantic area. Unfortunately the officials have had their hands tied by government policy.
Knowing the very real ability the minister has shown in private life and in his brief stint so far as a minister of the crown, I hope he will develop a policy with regional implications that will recognize the special problems of the Atlantic provinces, much though the mandarins abhor the suggestion that there are such special problems, and provide additional employment to an area that desperately needs it. I believe the minister can do this. As his personality gradually makes itself felt in this administration I look forward with anticipation to a time when he will put forward regional policies that will be truly valuable not only to the people of the Atlantic area but to all the people of Canada. Certainly any benefits that accrue to the people of the Atlantic provinces must at the same time accrue to all the people of Canada.

It is often the case that competitive bidding is not wholly satisfactory from the government point of view. Because of their personal association with members of the government of the day, persons such as I have described are able to convince the federal authorities that the groups they represent can offer the people of Canada the best that is available in a certain field of supply. As a result of these activities the taxpayers end up purchasing goods or equipment which may well not be the best available. It is considered the best, though, because it has been promoted by friends of the government.
This is a dangerous type of development of which every Canadian and, indeed, the government itself should be leary. I would not like to think that a certain firm employed officers who could write letters to people in Canada saying: I am having difficulty getting office space but until I am settled you can always contact me by telephoning the office of the Prime Minister or the office of the Minister of Transport. A persons getting a letter of that kind might well feel: I do not know whether my product is as good as others are but if I have the help of that individual, I am half way there so far as selling to the government is concerned.
I do not suggest for one minute that any cabinet minister or any government would consciously and deliberately favour a certain product simply because a particular group or individual was promoting it. But I do say there are many unconscious considerations, of which a partisan association over a period of time is certainly one, which a man is bound to look at more than once before he can obliterate them from his mind. I like to think there are many reasons why young men should be attracted to the many positions very close to the top which are available in the government service. I like to think these positions are a training ground for political scientists, for budding politicians. We applauded that decision, but actually very little has been done toward implementing the government's announced program. The performance of the government in this regard reminds me of the performance of some of the sports cars one sees throughout the country, not much speed but a great deal of noise.
I realize that the minister concerned with the safety program is the Minister of Transport. Every few weeks we ask him what is being done about setting up the public safety board as well as encouraging the work of the specifications people with regard to the components of the vehicles. We get very little in the way of a satisfactory reply.
I have received complaints from an automobile dealer in Ottawa to the effect he does not wish to sell a car which he is importing because there are no standards set for the safety of a three point seat belt. This car is equipped with such a seat belt but he does not want to sell it because he does not want to take the responsibility for marketing an article for which there is no specified standard of quality in Canada. This is his complaint to me. I urge the Minister of Defence Production, who has responsibility for the specifications board, to do all he can to speed up the activities of that body. If possible, perhaps he could go beyond that and encourage the Minister of Transport to spare some time from looking after harbours in Vancouver and housing across the country to
Supply-Supply and Services get some action in establishing the very necessary public safety board to deal with matters of automotive safety in Canada. I find it difficult to imagine anything that is more important or would save more lives than a better policy for traffic safety.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

May I answer a question that was asked earlier? I do not know whether the hon. member is in the house at the moment but I am sure he will get news of the answer. I said I was not sure what our involvement was with regard to the purchase of drugs. I am told we do buy all drugs for the Department of National Defence, Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of National Health and Welfare. In addition, we are quite prepared to discuss with other agencies, including provincial agencies, possible joint purchasing programs. This is a matter that is under review, and I gather some initial discussions in this regard are taking place.
My hon. friend who asked about the New Liskeard is no longer in the chamber so I will keep the answer to his question until later.

Mr. Chairman, I have a series of questions more than anything else at this stage of the minister's estimates. May I join with previous speakers in congratulating the minister on his new role and I wish him well. Many of us will be looking to him on a continuing basis as time goes by for answers to our questions.
The minister mentioned drugs, and I must not let the opportunity go by to ask those who purchase drugs not to get involved with counterfeit drugs about which I have been harping in this chamber for the last few weeks. I have indicated to the minister that there is sufficient of a contraband substance, which is the constituent of a very popular brand of drug made in Canada, in the hands, I understand, of the Mafia to produce some 10 million tablets. To date about 500,000 tablets have been recovered. I simply indicate that there are 9,500,000 of these tablets made from counterfeit drugs on the market. Whether this substance has all been converted to tablet form yet really does not matter because the conversion is very easy. However, I would ask the minister, in the interest of our veterans and hospitals across Canada, to exercise caution in this matter. The department purchases its supplies in bulk and it is very easy to slide in a few hundred thousand tablets of counterfeit drugs.
November 4, 1968

Supply-Supply and Services
The questions I want to ask today are fairly varied. I need not elaborate on them because I think the minister is familiar with at least one of the areas I am concerned about. I refer to the relationship between the government's defence purchasing agency and the plant of Fairey Aviation of Canada which is located at Eastern Passage, just outside the city of Dartmouth. I would ask the minister, at some later point in the discussion of his estimates, to bring the house up to date on a number of questions that were asked by representatives of the international association of machinists and aerospace workers. Members of the House of Commons were also present at the time in the minister's office. In this connection I am pleased to see the Minister of National Defence with us in the house.
There is one way in which these workers can receive assistance. I refer to working-out parties at the Canadian Forces base, Shearwater. I might point out that Fairey Aviation is a highly sophisticated and key industry within the metropolitan area of Halifax and Dartmouth, and must be sustained over what is going to be a rough period for the next two or three years.
Up to about two years ago a substantial number of workers not only from Fairey Aviation but from other related firms, such as electronics and radar manufacturers, in order to facilitate the work of the maintenance people within the armed forces at the naval air station were permitted to do technical jobs at the base. At times, this outside work force numbered, if my memory serves me correctly, in the order of 65 to 70 men. However, as a result of the cut-backs that were made during the last two years at Shearwater the situation has changed. In 1960, just eight years ago, 811 shopmen, that is to say, men working in the shop using tools and instruments-sheet metal workers, airframe and engine mechanics, painters and so on- worked at the base. Today there are 317 and actually that figure has been reduced further as of last Friday, though I do not have the exact number.
On the other hand, in the same year, 1960, there were 187 people employed in the management branch. Today there are 221. So we have the number employed on the management side growing and that on the workshop side reducing. I am not in any way suggesting that the company is in error here. Perhaps it is simply the result of the company endeavouring to build up a competent engineering and sales staff so that it can diversify

its production. As the minister is aware, the workers realize the necessity for the company moving away from total reliance on military purchases to the area of commercial production-to diversification, which I think is the word most commonly used today.
As I say, I should like the minister to bring me up to date on this situation. I also hope the Minister of National Defence is in a benevolent mood in this regard and will see fit to reintroduce work contracts, if only on a from time to time or interim basis. This will be one of the most useful and readily accessible tools to enable the Minister of Defence Production to assist the plant in sustaining itself over this most difficult two year period. It seems to me that two or three weeks ago an order did emanate from maritime command to employ a small working-out party composed of 12 or 14 men for a specific project at Shearwater.
The policy that has been in effect for, I imagine, about 18 of the 20 years in which Fairey Aviation has been located in this area seems a not unreasonable one, particularly in light of the alternatives. These are pretty straightforward: either close the plant down, or both management and union make an appeal to the government for work under a regional development program. This would involve a department not yet formed and assume policies not yet enunciated or, I suspect, completely thought out. I suggest that the first alternative is unthinkable in terms of its effect on the economy of the Dartmouth and Halifax county area. Its impact on the tax assessment rolls and on the corner store would be the same as anywhere else in Canada. Perhaps the minister would throw some light on this situation.
I would also be grateful if the minister would tell me whether or not he was successful in diverting any contracts for the Yukon aircraft from Canadair in Montreal. Certainly they would be very useful to Fairey Aviation.
The matter to which I now refer may not fall directly within the minister's purview but I would ask him to give me some explanation why competent aircraft inspection teams are finding that roughly 50 per cent of the recommended overhaul, repair and maintenance work is not being carried out by the air force at this time, particularly work on Argus aircraft. Is the reason simply shortage of money? Perhaps there are some specific modification programs that can be deferred without danger to the safety of the aircraft, the air frame, the engines or any of the radio-navigational aids on board.
November 4, 1968
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It is important that the Fairey matter be dealt with quickly. If it cannot be dealt with quickly we should be informed.
I want to know the present status of the general purpose DX program in the United States, as this has some relation to our participation under defence production sharing arrangements with regard to the bear trap or haul-down device for rotary winged aircraft. Perhaps the matter is classified and I shall therefore understand if it cannot be dealt with now. Perhaps the minister might tell us the present disposition of the bear trap program as it relates to our own four destroyer escorts. When may our plants anticipate receiving the benefits of this additional work? Is there a contract for it? Is there any competition? Also, will the addition of this instrument have any great impact on operations?
An earlier speaker touched on the McDon-nell-Douglas DC-10 program. I think the minister and Canadian industry generally are to be congratulated for the way in which the matter has been handled. This program is probably the largest single acquisition that has come our way for a long time. That is true, certainly, in the field of commercial aircraft. The dollar benefits are almost unpredictable. Engineers of the Canadian aircraft industry and individuals who took a leading role in this matter are to be congratulated for creating a proper atmosphere which was conducive to the favourable negotiations with the McDonnell-Douglas people. Though the Fairey people have a small part of this contract I wonder whether the minister could make sure that they receive some additional work under the program. I apologize for rambling on about Fairey aviation. Generally the aircraft industry in Canada is in a healthy state. Companies have diversified and are keeping busy. Most of them are expanding rapidly in the field of aircraft and aircraft components and allied fields. Unfortunately Fairey aviation appears to be the one company in Canada that is encountering trouble.
May I also ask the minister to bring us up to date on our four new DDH's-the words stand, I think, for destroyer and helicopter deployment. I have had trouble pronouncing them though we all know what they mean. On February 21 of this year I placed on the
Supply-Supply and Services order paper the following question which I shall read in part:
1.	What is the present total estimated cost for construction of the four new destroyers, including the equipment costs of these ships?
2.	When will the review of the bids for the construction of these ships be completed?
And so on. The minister replied that the estimated cost of construction is between $220 million and $225 million. I ask the minister whether that figure has changed since February 21, 1968. If so, in what quantity? Perhaps I should ask, what is the quality of the change? Have components been changed or have they become more expensive? If they have been changed, are the changes substantial? Have the minister's colleagues asked him to buy bigger and better equipment for the ships? An elementary question is, what type of propulsion unit is to power these ships? One type of unit was contemplated and a hull designed for it. Then the unit was changed, the one finally chosen being a gas turbine, I understand.

If the hon. member wishes perhaps I might resolve that matter quickly at this time. The hon. member quoted the figure that was given in answer to his question, between $220 million and $225 million for the four vessels, and that figure still stands. I am sure my hon. friend will not ask me to differentiate between a DDH-280 and a DDH-283. It is anticipated that two will be delivered in 1971, one in June and one in November, and the other two in 1972, one in June and the other in September. The propulsion units are gas turbines. I hope the hon. member will not ask me to go too deeply into the technical aspect. I know they are approved types of gas turbines to be supplied by United Aircraft of Canada Limited, in Quebec. The estimated price of the propulsion units is about $44.2 million.
Is that $44.2 million for the four vessels?
That is the total contract.
Has the minister been alerted to possible increases in the cost of this program?

No, Mr. Chairman. For once in our lives the estimate that was provided over one year ago is hanging pretty firm. I am advised that the total amount, as contained in the answer, is to be between $220 and $225 million or in that neighbourhood.

Not in the detail which the hon. member has suggested. However, in connection with the major items, about 167 contracts have been let for these four destroyers. The minister need not trouble to go over the whole list. Would he simply tell me how they were purchased?

I thank the minister for that information. There are other detailed questions I should like to ask but I shall wait until we get off the generalities of item one. I will ask this question in the light of Admiral O'Brien's remarks in Halifax over the week end when he

expressed concern about our present ability to meet our commitments. I should also like to ask the minister later about the hydrofoil program, and whether or not the hon. gentleman and his colleague, the Minister of National Defence, are any closer to a decision about the refueling tanker, or the role of the CF-5. Mr. Chairman, allow me
to make a few remarks about the estimates under consideration this afternoon.
The study of that department's estimates reminds me of a question I asked last Friday.
I was wondering if any attention was paid to the reports of the experts who stated that a saving of $10 million was possible should the maintenance base for jet airplanes in Winnipeg be closed and transferred to Montreal. I hope that this needless expenditure which would be incurred if the base were maintained will be considered because it has been asked that it be phased out gradually until 1973.
I hope that the department representatives will accept to meet the members of the Q.F.L. to discuss the recommendations made by the committees of experts. We receive at our offices reports and studies of all kinds and if, after the statements by the experts, the need to make those studies over again is felt, there will be no end to all that, and I feel that the fact that a saving of $10 million can be made by moving the base from Winnipeg to Montreal will weigh heavily in favour of that move.
Like the member who spoke before me, I should also like to draw the attenton of the house to the Lauzon shipyard. I know it well, for several of my friends and relatives work there. We were not indifferent to the human tragedy that occurred there in 1967-68. We kept hoping that the member for Levis (Mr. Guay), would mention to the house the disaster which left over 1,000 workers unemployed. The situation is odd for two miles further up the river from the shipyard known as "le petit chantier"-since the Davie Shipbuilding yard is still in operation-which belonged to Canadian Vickers and was sold to Davie Shipbuilding, there is the Levis ferry-boat
November 4, 1968
crossing. Ferry-boats would be needed there to transport cars between the two shores without some cars having to wait, as long as two hours sometimes, on the Quebec side as well as on the Levis side.
Now, while workers at Lauzon are looking for work because they refused to go to Newfoundland-after having lived there for 20, 25 years, with their families, their friends, their common heritage, they did not want to leave Lauzon-there is a shortage of boats nearby, and subsidies are not even made available to provide for larger and faster ferry-boats between Levis and Quebec. Some of the ferry-boats now being used were built in 1927 and in winter they cannot take more than 25 cars at one time when, in fact, 1,000 cars per hour should cross from one side of the river to the other.
Here is an example of what goes on in that part of the province: last Friday, it took me one hour and ten minutes to fly from Ottawa to the airport at L'Ancienne Lorette; it took me exactly one hour and fifteen minutes to cross the Quebec bridge, on my way from the airport at L'Ancienne Lorette to Saint-Nicholas. We put up with that because the ferry-boats between Quebec and Levis cannot take cars for lack of space. Everyone uses the Quebec bridge and the situation is deplorable.
There are anomalies, such as stupid statements of which, amongst others, that were made last week by the member for Quebec East (Mr. Duquet) who spoke instead of the Grande Hermine. He did not know where the Grande Hermine was hiding. He went to Montreal then to Quebec, to be told by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) that instead of giving work to the labourers at the Lauzon shipyard, the Grande Hermine would finally be taken to Lauzon, and winter there. They are trying to save face by talking about the many advantages of the proposed Cartier-Brebeuf park, but nothing is done to diminish the unemployment which affects many families on the south shore.

Unfortunately, the hon. member for Levis has not yet expressed his views. We, on this side of the house, expected him to mention this deplorable situation. I see that he is not in the house today-incidentally, he is not here very often-and the people of his riding must often think that they might as well not have a representative in parliament. Unfortunately, my friends believe that silence should be kept concerning situations of this sort.

while we in Canada, thanks to the St. Lawrence which is open to ships of all nations could have built up a merchant marine of our own which we would still have and which would prevent a few individuals from getting rich at Canada's expense.
In closing, after these few remarks, I ask a question to which I hope I shall get an answer. How can we explain the transfer to Newfoundland of the Lauzon shipyards in an attempt to force our Lauzon workers to go and work in Newfoundland which, for us Quebecers, almost means a deportation.
We, on the south shore, judge as abnormal such a deportation of workers to Newfoundland. We would rather ask that shipyards such as those in Lauzon continue to be prosperous as they were during the war.

Mr. Chairman, I hope that in his native tongue the hon. gentleman was not using the word that came through in translation. I am sure he did not mean to suggest that people from Lauzon are being deported to Newfoundland. We are a little removed yet from the category of Devil's Island.

The minister might wait until tomorrow to read my statement to the effect that the Lauzon workers who were forced to go and earn their living in Newfoundland on account of the subsidies granted to that province thought they were deported.

Mr. Chairman, on rising to speak on the estimates of the new department of supply and services I also offer congratulations and best wishes to the minister, but as a new member and a comparatively modest businessman I am a wee bit suspicious of the words he used today in explaining how he

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I hope he will give sympathetic consideration to a petition forwarded by the citizens of Stephenville who are facing the disposal of the Air Canada terminal building there by the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. When he receives their brief I hope he will decide not to dispose of the terminal building to anyone but the citizens of Stephenville.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member would like to qualify his opening gambit. For the record, what he quoted was probably essentially correct but to some extent it was lifted out of context. However, that is beside the point. I am not aware of any petition which has reached my office yet, but I can assure him that it will receive every consideration. May I ask the hon. member whether it is due to arrive shortly?
I have a copy in my hand. It was given to me as I left to return to Ottawa. I think the minister's copy is on the way but if it would help I am willing to lend him the copy I have.

In a general way the Glassco commission was fairly critical of the Crown

Assets Disposal Corporation in its present form. The minister did not mention the corporation in his opening statement and I would like him to enlighten the committee on his intentions with regard to this agency.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I guess I ought to apologize for not referring to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The reason I did not is that there is not a particular vote with regard to it, and I was merely looking at the different headings in the estimates. A number of suggestions put forward from time to time with regard to the corporation, including suggestions by the Glassco commission, have been implemented. I am satisfied that present procedures are an improvement on what they were previously. We have a very aggressive general manager in crown assets today. He, along with the president of the board, has been reviewing their techniques and procedures. A good deal has been done. For myself I am not entirely happy that we have got the optimum situation yet. I have begun a series of reviews with crown assets on their methods and practices with a view to increasing the corporation's productivity and its returns to the Canadian taxpayer.
The hon. member for Central Nova asked me a question about the New Liskeard. This vessel was to be phased out and there was a time lag between the time she would no longer be serviceable and the time when her replacement, The Quest, now under construction, would be ready. It was determined in the first instance that the amount of work intended to be done on her was really too costly in reference to the length of time she would be in service. Therefore the decision was made not to proceed with her repair and overhaul.
Subsequently it was suggested that there might be a period during which she would have to be employed before The Quest was ready, and so absolutely minimal repair and overhaul proposals were made. Again in a third phase, as The Quest program was stepped up and it became evident that this vessel would be available more quickly, it was decided not to proceed with any expensive repairs.
The hon. member for Frontenac made reference to Mrs. Kennedy purchasing a vessel from us previously. Mr. Chairman, I would be only too glad to enter into negotiations with her about the New Liskeard in a few months.

Mr. Chairman, I have been trying to get in a question all afternoon. I had not realized that my hon. friends were so adept in presenting their viewpoints, and I had figured that these estimates would have been passed quite some time ago.
We were all impressed by the minister's opening statement. He showed by his attitude that he is very capable of running his department. We are also happy that the Minister of National Defence has the attitude he has toward the eastern part of Canada. He has been very co-operative with my colleagues on several matters. The question I wish to ask is not directly related to the minister's department. I am thinking of the national defence training base in the most easterly Canadian province. Some time ago questions were asked of the minister about Russian activities off the east coast of Canada. These aroused quite a bit of interest in the eastern part of Canada. We on the east coast are always a little leary of Russian activity and we recognize a need to step up defence activity on the eastern seaboard.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Second, we perhaps are a little bit-how should I put it-unhappy about the fact that despite the billion dollars which is being spent in Canada annually under the Department of Defence Production and I suppose the Department of National Defence very little of this money actually is being channelled into the easterly province to which I am referring.
I wonder whether the Minister of Defence Production or the Minister of National Defence would ract to the reasonable suggestion that a national defence training base be established in the province of Newfoundland in view of the recent activities by Russia- and in view of the fact that it would stimulate the economy of that area.

Mr. Chairman, earlier in the debate I quoted some figures concerning employment in the Canadian shipbuilding industry. At that time I believe I stated that the figure fell from 17,000 to 9,000. I believe the minister is aware of the publication from which I took this information. It is a chart of the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repair association. The figure of 17,000 was in the year 1952. This has not been the average figure for years. I know that the figure for 1961 was 10,000. In the last two years it was 12,893, nearly 13,000. As of July of this year it was 9,603. Furthermore, I have figures from the association which show that as of August this year the average employment in Canadian shipyards was 8,995. So there would appear to be quite a decline. I just wanted to straighten out the figures for the record.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a supplementary question concerning the sale of the centennial caravans through the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. Is the previous practice of putting materials up for tender still in effect?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. This is one of the matters which I suggested I would investigate further in order to determine whether or not we could improve this method. There is no deviation from the tender process. As the hon. member knows, certain agencies, first of all the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities, have priority. This system is in effect, but there may be room for improvement and we are examining it. It may be that the bulk system is the best way to do it or it might be that there could be some improvement whereby smaller firms, if not individuals, might have access to some of these materiels. But the basic program and policy are as the hon. member stated.

Mr. Chairman, my purpose is not to follow the minister in his quest for the New Liskeard, but I should like to wish him well in his negotiations to sell the New Liskeard to Mrs. Onassis when it has served its purpose in the naval environment of the Canadian armed forces. As members perhaps know, Mr. Onassis bought a Canadian warship previously and transformed it into a yacht. If the minister is successful in selling

DEBATES	November 4, 1968
the New Liskeard to the former Jackie Kennedy, Mr. Onassis would simply have to paint out the name on his yacht and they could be marked "his" and "hers" in order to differentiate.
There would seem to be a fair maritime flavour about the debate. Like my colleagues I wish to join in wishing the minister well. I do not think too many people realize this, but I believe it should be on record that he was the one candidate for his party in that province who put himself forward to a nominating convention. He was also the one candidate who escaped the avalanche of common sense which otherwise swept over Newfoundland. So I suggest we have here a figure to be reckoned with. Probably the most powerful Newfoundland Liberal is the one who now sits in this chamber. I do not know whether he has pretensions about going back home but in any event we wish him well.
My purpose in rising is to support the request of my colleague the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East with regard to the Fairey Aviation Company and also to utter a bit of a caveat to the minister with regard to his plowshare philosophy. Generally speaking I think this is a fine philosophy, but it has its hazards and pitfalls. After all, defence spending is one of the weapons available to our society as it exists now for spreading out economic benefits to the less developed parts of Canada. I believe it is a useful weapon in the war on regional disparity.
The idea behind our thinking in respect of the Fairey Aviation Company is that we might be able to provide the greater Halifax-Dartmouth area with technicians and people of other skills. Besides being of help to an area where there is regional disparity this would be a useful equalizer so that everything does not wind up in the Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto golden triangle. Therefore, as the minister adopts his plowshare philosophy I hope he will hold something in reserve until new and different programs or approaches appear as alternatives to the decentralized spending of the defence dollar. I hope he will not advance his theory too far but if he can bring it into being, more power to him.

I will have to take notice of that question in view of its importance rather
