speakeroldname: Mr. Roberl C. Coales (Cumberland-Col-cesler Norlh) moved:
subtopic: CHIGNECTO COMPLEX-SUGGESTED CONSTRUCTION OF DAMS AND CANAL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give immediate consideration to the construction of the Chignecto complex, with the construction of dams on the Minas Basin, Cumberland Basin and Shepody Bay and the construction of the Chignecto Canal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is often said that it never rains but it pours, and certainly this would apply today so far as this subject is concerned. I never miss an opportunity to place before members of this house the problems which we face in the Atlantic provinces and some of the ways in which I feel we might be able to find solutions to them.
It is my belief that in this session we have often spent a great deal of time talking about things over which we have little or no control, such as the civil war in Nigeria, and all too little time facing up to the problems over which we do have control if we would only do something about them. I witnessed with a great deal of interest the federal-provincial conference held in February in which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took such an active part. I listened to his comments about regional economic dispartity in Canada. I heard him repeat them when he sought the leadership of his party last April. I listened once again to discussion of the problems created by regional economic disparity during the election campaign. Yet I come to this house and I am still waiting for the government and the ministers responsible to take some obvious action which will help to eliminate these problems which everyone seems to recognize but which unfortunately no one in the present government appears really to be determined to do anything about.
One of the things that shocked me as a member from the Atlantic provinces was the fact that the Prime Minister would not give special priority to the establishment of a special department about which he talked so much. I am sure that the people of the Atlantic region are becoming more and more disillusioned as each day passes with no indication from the government that it is ready to move forward in the fashion which we had anticipated from the statements of the Prime Minister.
The motion before us, if adopted, would eliminate many of the arguments which I anticipate will be put forward when the final
Water Resources
studies are completed on the engineering feasibility of the construction of dams to harness the tides to produce power in the bay of Fundy. I do not think there is any doubt that the project in question must be feasible for it is obvious that in France they have harnessed the tides and as a result they are now the beneficiaries of the power which is available from this source.
I have learned from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Saturday, October 26, that the Severn river tidal power plant project in Great Britain is being seriously considered, for they too realize the value of harnessing the tides to obtain power.
For a long period of time I pressed the former Liberal administration to try to get them to initiate studies, but it was only after a great deal of procrastination on their part that a body was finally established in co-operation with the governments of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I understand that the project for the construction of the dams is going forward as fast as possible, but what concerns me is that as soon as the study is completed we will begin hearing arguments about the economic feasibility of the project and about whether or not money of the government of Canada should be invested in a project in the Atlantic provinces. This concerns me because we are the afterthought area of Canada. After everything is done that is required in the other six provinces of Canada the crumbs are brushed off the table for the four Atlantic provinces and we are told: this is good enough for you fellows down there.
This has been the philosophy for 100 years, and in this regard the present government does not appear to be different from the last government. When they were talking about cutting down expenditures, one of the first big cuts of which we became aware was the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway. In other words, when projects are put on the cutting table they look at the Atlantic provinces first to see what they can take away from them because there are fewer of them and therefore they need not worry about the mess, especially these days when most of the members from that area belong to another political party. This is the sad fact.
As a matter of fact, the premier of Prince Edward Island came here with his 15 cabinet ministers to make representations to the Prime Minister, and it is my understanding that the Prime Minister had only six minutes available in which to hear the premier on this very

November 4, 1968
Water Resources
important transportation link in our area. But this is not something new; it is the old philosophy which has been in existence ever since confederation. It is the kind of philosophy that will do damage to the possibilities we have available in the Atlantic provinces with the harnessing of the Fundy tides.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
With these Fundy tides there is another logical project that should follow and that is the Chignecto canal. At the time the St. Lawrence seaway was being built for central Canada we told the people of Canada that we should have the natural extension of the St. Lawrence seaway, the Chignecto canal. The St. Lawrence seaway was built but we are still waiting for the Chignecto canal. Last session I wanted to ascertain just what the people of Canada were asked to invest in the St. Lawrence seaway. Since we are part of Canada, some of our tax dollars went to provide this more efficient method for shipping into central Canada. The figure with which I was provided indicated that the people of Canada expended a total of $541,940,000, or 80 per cent of the total cost. The United States invested $131,054,000. The total cost of the project was $672,994,000. The important factor is not that we spent that kind of money to build the St. Lawrence seaway but that prior to its construction we were told of the great benefits that were going to accrue to Canada, that it would be a paying proposition and there would be no difficulty in getting a return of the invetment that we made as taxpayers of this nation.
In the same question I asked how the principal was being retired. I was told that payments have been made only to the extent of a portion of the interest accrued and therefore there were arrears. In other words, not only is the principal not being retired on the St. Lawrence seaway debt but we are not even getting enough from the tolls to pay the interest. We were led to believe that there was no doubt this would be a paying proposition and that the people of Canda had no need to fear about their tax dollars because they would be returned. I have no argument about the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. I think it was a valuable thing for this nation to have this modern form of transportation available. What I say is, should not we in the Atlantic provinces have a right to expect similar treatment of the kind of projects we have available?

Certainly the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway is one of those projects we should expect to be constructed because it will be of benefit to the people of Canada. For one thing, the completion of this project would eliminate the huge deficits the taxpayers of this nation are required to meet each year to provide transportation facilities for the people in this area.
One of the really serious things this government should consider when it is talking about regional disparity, when it is talking about equality of opportunity, when it is talking about the just society, is that we in the Atlantic provinces should be provided with the same opportunities as everyone else. One of the suggestions that concerns me most in the submission made by Premier G. I. Smith of Nova Scotia to the federal-provincial conference in February is the suggestion that while we move ahead we move backwards at the same time. These are the figures that are so frightening from the Atlantic provinces' point of view. Mr. Smith is talking about regional economic disparity and he says:
The chief available statistical measure that shows the economic disparity between Nova Scotia and the rest of the nation is per capita personal income. To illustrate the seriousness of this gap we wish to draw the conference's attention to the following examples: In 1961 Nova Scotia's per capita income was $1,097 or 76.5 per cent of the Canadian average. In 1966 per capita income had risen in Nova Scotia to $1,583, 74.2 per cent of the Canadian average.
The important figure is not the amount of money but the percentage. The percentage of the Canadian average was 76.5 per cent in 1961 and 74.2 per cent in 1966. In other words, in those five years we fell farther behind while having more money in our pockets. We fell farther behind by 2.3 per cent. If this trends continues, God knows what is going to happen to the area. There is no hope for the Atlantic provinces of Canada unless we have from the federal government the kind of policies that will eliminate regional economic disparity. Up to the moment there has been little indication from the government that it is taking the problem as seriously as one would have expected from the statements made by the Prime Minister during the period of time he was running for office. What we have to do now is get on with the job, get these projects under way.
While the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) can tell us the amount of money being spent for training and retraining the people in that part of Canada, there is not much value in the training from
November 4, 1968

an area point of view if as soon as the people become trained they go to other parts of Canada for employment. We are not interested in becoming the training ground for workers for the remainder of this nation. But that, Mr. Speaker, is the sad situation today. There just is no choice for our workers. We have to have projects that will go along with the training. Then we will be happy; then we will know we can live wherever we wish to live and have equality of opportunity. This is what this government has not produced and I hope that in the days ahead there will be more indication of action, more indication that it is endeavouring to do something about some of the things over which we have control and less talk about what is going to be available in the just society 15 years hence. We are interested in what the government is going to do today, not what it is going to produce for us 15 years from now. We are waiting for this government to move.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
subtopic: CHIGNECTO COMPLEX-SUGGESTED CONSTRUCTION OF DAMS AND CANAL
speechtext:
The hon. member who put this motion on the order paper, Mr. Speaker, has used it as a narrow base from which to deal in a broad fashion with 'the subject of regional development. I think this is a proper matter for us to talk about in this chamber this evening. I am not suggesting it was not in order to do so; I think it was quite in order that he should broaden his remarks as he did.
I am very pleased that he did so because it gives me, and I hope my colleagues on this side of the house, the opportunity to deal for a few minutes with some of the projects and plans of the government in the field of regional development.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
Before I do this, Mr. Speaker, let me comment for a moment or two about the launching pad for our debate this evening, if I may call it such, the motion that is specifically before Your Honour for debate. The hon. member who put the motion on the order paper seems to suggest that this house should ask the government to proceed with a project without really taking the opportunity to assess the feasibility and financial consequences thereof.
I do not think my hon. friend would want the government of Canada or indeed, as he properly pointed out, the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, all three of whom are engaged in a study that is being carried out by the tidal powers programming 29180-152
Water Resources
board, to embark upon such a project now. As the house knows, this board is investigating the physical and economic potential of the development of electric power from the tides of the bay of Fundy and the transmission of this power to markets in Canada and the United States.
This is an investigation that is, as I say, being carried on by all three governments and will provide a realistic assessment of the feasibility of tidal power development in the Atlantic region and its potential effect on other aspects of area development, including among other things the Chignecto canal. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, putting the matter on that rather narrow base, I think we should reasonably and realistically wait until this investigation has been concluded and we have the board's report.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, because all hon. members will agree that we cannot do everything we want to do as quickly as we would like. By "we", I mean those of us at the federal and provincial levels who are concerned with regional disparity. Therefore some priorities have to be established, and it is important that the governments concerned wait for the board's report. In the meantime, and indeed after the report has been received and assessed, we should try to establish priorities so that the not inexhaustible amount of money involved can best be spent in correcting regional disparities particularly in the Atlantic provinces.
I think my hon. friend has probably read the remarks made by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) in Halifax a week ago tomorrow night when he spoke to the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. I think it would be timely for us to talk of regional development at this time because we can do so in the context of the minister's remarks about the sort of broad area of operation that he foresees for his department.
With respect, Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend was being a little unduly critical in suggesting that nothing was being done by the department in this regard. I should like to take a minute or two to refer to some of the things the minister said in Halifax last week, and also to mention that although the legislation has not been presented to the house yet-again, it is a question of priorities; we have been dealing with other very important legislation-the minister did say the other day that it would be presented as quickly as

November 4, 1968
Water Resources
possible, or at least pretty soon. It is, as I say, a question of priorities.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, the department is not at a standstill. Under the other legislative authority that we have, the Government Organization Act, the minister and his officials have been putting together this new department, and since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) expressed his intention of setting up this new department a good deal has been done.
I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, the question of priorities in determining the projects about which we should be thinking for the Atlantic provinces, as well as the necessity for waiting for the report of the board. May I refer for a few moments to the minister's speech which he delivered at Halifax. In dealing with the question of priorities in regional development he had this to say:
That realization has brought us to phase three in the history of regional development, represented at the federal level by the decision to set up a new department with comprehensive responsibility for planning and co-ordinating action for regional development.
That involves much more than the federation of existing programs, in order to eliminate duplication and improve government efficiency. I don't undervalue that. But there is much more to our objectives.
The new department is being created essentially because regional development is a matter of top priority for the federal government.
"If the under-development of the Atlantic provinces is not corrected-not by charitty or subsidies but by helping them become areas of economic growth-then the unity of the country is almost as surely destroyed as it would be by the French-English confrontation."
The minister then went on to say:
Those are the words of the Prime Minister, and there are many more to the same effect.
That indicates, Mr. Speaker, the importance of priorities and indeed the importance placed by the Prime Minister on the work of this department.
In dealing with the task before the department, in his speech to APEC in Halifax last week the minister had this to say:
We have to see that the forces of economic demand operate more consistently across the country. Or, to put it in another way, our job is to see that economic growth is dispersed widely enough across the country to provide equal access to opportunities of productive employment for Canadians everywhere.
That is what I mean by a regional development policy. I mean that the federal government is prepared to take special action where it is needed to bring opportunities up to standard. Broad national policies for employment are not enough. And it is not sufficient just to add to them a
[Mr. Honey.1
variety of area plans and agencies. There has to be a comprehensive structuring of government action to regional needs.
I was with the minister on his visit to the Atlantic provinces last week, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to put this proposition to the hon. member who sponsored this motion.
I suggest there would not be anything like majority agreement in the Atlantic provinces with some of the suggestions he made in his remarks a few minutes ago. I had the opportunity of talking to the people there and I do not think that they would agree with his appellation of them as "have-not" provinces. All of us who are responsible for trying to even out opportunities and incentives in this country are doing the best we can. We may not all be perfect, of course, and other governments prior to this government have tried to do their best. Nevertheless there is always room for criticism. The general impression that I gathered from spending two days in the Atlantic provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia-and I believe the minister to whom I am responsible shares this view-is that the provincial governments and the federal government are working well together.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
There was, indeed, a great concentration of effort to assist the Atlantic provinces, and perhaps I might be permitted to indicate some of the things this government and its immediate predecessor have done in that direction. I do not want to be overly critical of my hon. friend who sponsored the motion, but his remarks leave the implication that little has been done.

As a seconder of the motion I wish to indicate my support for it. The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North deserves credit for bringing forward this question again. He has been persistent and consistent over the years, both when he was in the government party and out of it. He has supported the subject matter of this motion and has put his thoughts on the record in a clearcut way.
I was pleased to hear that the parliamentary secretary attended with the minister the recent meeting of APEX in Halifax, but I am sorry he did not display more enthusiasm. He seems to reflect an attitude that has been prevalent for the short time this government has been in power, that of stalling on reports, looking into this and that, and trying to break promises. We would have been more pleased had the parliamentary secretary returned from his trip to the maritimes and said in this house: I am sorry about conditions in the maritimes; I am sympathetic; I will do all I can; I do not know the details, perhaps, but I am in favour of doing something to bring the

just society to the maritimes. Instead, he tells us that the government needs to wait for another report. He says: We must look into this; we have to know where we are going. It is the same story; it goes on and on.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
I want to say there have been many reports on this Chignecto project and every one of them to my knowledge has been favourable. As a matter of fact, in 1891 there was a full communications system built up over this canal; the remains of the old Chignecto railway are still there today. We realize that it takes a long time for projects to sink in. Even the Prince Edward Island causeway idea took a long time before the government accepted it, and started to work on it. Now that the causeway is almost completed we think hon. gentlemen opposite should turn their minds to another project.
I know there are many other hon. members who wish to speak; this is one of the most enthusiastic private members hours I have seen for a long while. I hope that members other than maritimers will support this motion. In conclusion, I voice once again my support for the canal project, and the power project which in itself is bigger then even the Churchill falls scheme. With nine million horsepower at three mills it is better than Churchill falls. I hope the government will stand up for its principles, abide by its election promises and get right on with this tomorrow. Let us not find these pre-election promises turning into post-election corpses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first
occasion upon which I have had the responsibility of bringing before the house the estimates of the Department of Public Works. I
November 4, 1968

want to thank members in advance for the kind consideration I know they are going to give me. I say this in lively anticipation of further favours to come.
I think it would be well if I were to say a few words about the general reasoning behind the estimates of the Department of Public Works in this current year. It has been the desire of the government to cool somewhat the inflationary tendencies that we have found in the economy, and probably particularly in the construction industry. At the same time we are fully aware that we cannot cool inflationary tendencies to the point where unemployment is aggravated or to the point where we fail to supply the requirements either directly on our own initiative or on behalf of other departments. I do not think we have done that in the current year.
It would be false economy, for example, to suspend completely the construction of office accommodation. In the long run this could only add an additional burden on the taxpayers, because the ultimate result would be to force up rentals to an exorbitant level. The office accommodation problem is always with us. No matter what we do, its solution usually seems to be a good long jump ahead of us. Populations in the nation grow and governments grow. Buildings become obsolete in some instances, and new types of accommodation such as buildings with strengthened floors to support the weight of the paper needed to feed data processing systems are required. We find a new situation in respect of the employees of the government. At every level of government we find the situation where employees no longer want to work in gloomy or airless accommodation or in surroundings that were typical of office buildings a half century ago. There has been a very marked upgrading of accommodation in the Public Service of Canada.
There are several approaches to the accommodation problem, all of which are reflected in the current estimates. One is to bring existing accommodation up to modern standards by introducing air conditioning and up to date lighting and generally refurbishing the office workers' surroundings. The other three ways, in increasing order of costs, are to build our own office accommodation, as we are doing in respect of the general purpose office building now rising at Tunney's Pasture, to enter into build-lease arrangements with the construction industry or to rent existing accommodation.
Supply-Public Works
It is hoped that substantial economies in crown construction will result from the adoption of modular co-ordination, which involves the use of standardized units in planning and standardized measurements in the production of building material. I should like to pay a tribute to the department, in that I think it has taken a very commendable leadership in the development of modular co-ordination in the last couple of years.
You will have observed from the estimates that the amount we are spending on harbour and river development has shown a decrease. Some very desirable projects have had to be postponed, but we have been able to retain other important works such as the St. Charles river control structure, Matane harbour, the development of Long Harbour, Newfoundland, and the New Westminster trifurcation project. No interruption has taken place in respect of those very important public works. In the case of the New Westminster trifurcation project, this project should be completed during the coming fiscal year and should result in significant long term savings in the form of reduced annual dredging costs.
The house is aware that a major harbour, capable of handling giant tankers, is being developed at Point Tupper, Nova Scotia. The work will be carried out by the Department of Public Works. This year the engineering plant is well under way in preparation for tender calls in the new year. This, in addition to the already mentioned Long Harbour project, is following a relatively new pattern in the assistance by the Department of Public Works of the development of major resources. These and certain other large harbour projects are subject to capital recapture from the mam beneficiaries. This is a trend we have been following in recent years whereby a public works project gives advantage, or contributes in a major way, to the economy of the country. The government has, in other words, advanced for the companies involved the amount of capital required to build docks and wharves. As I have said, this capital requirement in the first instance is recoverable.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The fast developing program of mineral exploration in the north, particularly with reference to oil and gas, accents the role of the Mackenzie river as a main transportation route. The department's dredging fleet in the Mackenzie basin is being used to maximum advantage and such major obstacles to river

November 4, 1968
Supply-Public Works transportation as the Sans Sault rapids are being eliminated.
Along the northwest highway system, many of the bridges built around the end of the second world war are being replaced under a program costing about $2 million a year. I am speaking of the Alaska highway. In some cases these bridges have reached the end of their useful lives, and in others they were under designed to handle modern traffic. Additionally, a dust abatement assessment program is being carried out in the vicinity of towns through which the Alaska highway passes.
About the time I was appointed Minister of Public Works it was announced that the Canadian government exhibition commission would be transferred to this department. The transfer was completed in September and accounts for an increase of some $5 million in our estimates for the current year.
In line with the recommendations of the Glassco commission and following a survey of departmental functions and operations by a management consultant group, a new organizational structure was devised for the department. Since a year ago last April the department has been operating under a decentralized system, with much of the authority formerly concentrated in headquarters delegated to six regions and 18 districts across the country.
I want to pay a compliment to my predecessor in this post. I think this decentralization aspect and the presence of the government of Canada in these regions and the districts of Canada is a very forward movement. I should like to compliment my predecessor the present Solicitor General for taking this action. A great number of our clients and contractors in the country, and probably a considerable number of members of parliament, are still not aware that the authority granted to these various districts is almost equal to that which could be obtained from our headquarters in Ottawa.
It is my hope that members of parliament will use these district heads from now on in respect of the work going on in the various districts, because the authority granted to these district heads is almost equivalent to that which exists here in Ottawa.
The advantages of decentralization have already become obvious to the department. In placing more authority closer to where the action is taking place our reactions have become faster and there is an increased aware-

ness of local needs. Our performance will continue to improve as the remaining problems in respect of the reorganization are solved.
What I have said gives the committee in the most general terms some of the objectives and problems of the department in the current year. I shall endeavour to see that hon. members are provided with complete and accurate answers to any questions which might arise from a study of the estimates now before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have the opportunity to comment on the estimates of the Department of Public Works now before us. I welcome the minister to this post and I hope that his department under his direction will be in a position to do more planning and exercise more foresight than has been the case in the past.
I have already suggested, in my maiden speech, that we should have long term planning. There appears to have been a lack of planning in this and other departments, and perhaps there is also a lack of co-operation. Let me give a good example of what I have in mind.
The National Arts Centre was first estimated to cost about $9 million. This cost was re-estimated at $18 million, but it will now reach something in the order of $46 million. Something must have gone wrong somewhere.
I am not against an arts centre but I am against extravagance at a time when this sort of money could be put to much better and more practical uses. It could have been spent to improve the marine facilities for fishermen. I do not blame the minister in this regard, since he is new to this department, but I hope such things can be avoided in the future.
Let me give another example. According to reports I received today the town of Rock Island in Quebec is to have a new post office, despite the fact there have been many objections raised. It has been suggested that the present post office is perfectly adequate and that the reason for building is to provide cafeteria facilities for the four people employed by the post office. Apparently the government is desperate to build a post office at this location.
It has also been brought to my attention today that 26 post offices in Nova Scotia will be closed beginning Ocotober 21, 1968 and carrying on into 1969. Four of those post
November 4, 1968

offices are in my constituency, and I am wondering whether this is justified. I should like to suggest to the department that a new post office be constructed at Parkers Cove. Perhaps the money allotted for the construction of the project at Rock Island could be devoted to some other use.
There obviously is a lack of planning and I hope the new minister will correct this situation. Many large fishing boats have been constructed in the past few years, particularly following the introduction a few years ago of subsidies in respect of wooden ships. These ships have been constructed, but wharves have not been improved or constructed to cope with the increased number and size of the ships. Perhaps there has been a lack of co-operation between the two departments concerned.
In my part of the country we do not have one good deep water harbour. Many fishing boats have been constructed in this area, but why has no major improvement in wharf and dock facilities taken place? The government has paid subsidies on the construction of these boats, yet facilities capable of accommodating them have not been provided. There appears again to have been no planning in this regard.
It is not my suggestion to the minister, as I said in my maiden speech, that every little village should be provided with a new wharf or breakwater. I do suggest in respect of southwestern Nova Scotia that we should maintain and preserve present wharves and breakwaters, while at the same time developing deep water harbours perhaps every 50 miles.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
For example, in Annapolis county in Nova Scotia there is a need for at least one deep water harbour. There has been some talk along these lines for many years, and fishermen in the Parkers Cove area have asked for one deep water harbour for many years. The policy seems to have been not to do anything to improve some of these facilities and finally to say that it costs too much to repair them. I think the fishermen would be content if we were to maintain and preserve the present structures that we have, and every so often make any necessary improvements. The same applies to the town of Annapolis which has a large export business of lumber, and pulp-wood. The government told one area in my riding that they cannot have a wharf in every little village. I am referring mainly to
Supply-Public Works wharves simply because about 95 per cent of my constituents depend on fisheries. The government told these people that they should try to get together to plan their action, and that when they do so the government will be prepared to go ahead with it.
This has happened in one instance in the Cape Sable Island area. The people got together and decided it was necessary to go ahead with the construction of a wharf at West Head, but the position of the government was that they had no money and could not do this work. Yet the people followed the advice of the government and did what was asked of them. This is another example of what I say is lack of planning on the part of the government.
In my constituency we have 63 breakwaters and 80 wharves, or 25 per cent of all the wharves and breakwaters in Nova Scotia. One good deep water port is required every 50 miles along the coastline of the constituency. There is a need for a deep water port in Pubnico and the Wedgeport area, since the Yarmouth port is not adequate. I will have more to say on this when we come to the details of the vote. For example, Wedgeport has been promised a wharf for many years. We hear the same story in every election, but no action is taken. Last year a wharf broke down in my constituency in Pinkney's Point. This year we find nothing in the estimates to cover the cost of rebuilding it, yet last year it was considered essential. This is what I mean by lack of planning.
In another instance, money was voted last year for a wharf in my constituency, yet no work was done. I could go on to mention every little village and town in my constituency where a wharf is needed but no work is being done. I know the minister is aware of the situation in the Digby area. I am sure he knows there is need for action with regard to a combination regional harbour for an efficient fleet, and there is also need for a permanent crossing. This has been recommended in a report.
During the last election the Liberal candidate in my riding said that the federal government was ready to go ahead with this, but that the provincial government did not want to take any action in this respect. However, my information is different. The one place in which the Prime Minister made a promise during the election campaign was in my constituency respecting the port of Digby. I refer to the $17 million project to improve ferry facilities between Digby and Saint John. The

November 4, 1968
Supply-Public Works project was to include $7 million for the construction of a new vessel and $10 million for docking and other facilities.
On looking through the estimates I found that half a million dollars was allocated for Digby and $475,000 for Saint John. At this rate it will take ten years for this project to be completed, and yet it has been promised. It has been said many times in the house that there is a need for improved facilities here, and that we will get them soon; yet nothing is being done now, and work will not be started for another couple of years.
This is another example of lack of planning. People are promised things and the promises are not kept. Quite a number of people are employed in the handling of freight at Digby and Saint John. What will happen to these people when the new vessel is constructed? I imagine that many will be out of work, so let us provide an alternative for them.
Let me remind the government of some of their promises given at a meeting in Digby, at which one of the speakers said there is a need for improved transportation facilities and larger wharves, and stressed the need for more adequate harbourage. According to what Dr. Stewart, the Liberal candidate in my riding, told the audience, if the government of Nova Scotia decides there is a necessity for a deep water crossing it should participate in the design work so that any project for marine harbour facilities will be as useful as possible. Again, at another meeting it was said that marine facilities are the backbone of the economy in our area. We must strive for continual improvement of these facilities if we are to have a fair share of the ocean resources available to us. This was stressed not by myself but by my opponent who was then parliamentary secretary to the minister. I wish that some of the funds could be reallocated or divided in a fair way. We have been told there would be a ferry in a few months time. The few months have gone by, but the tenders are not out yet, although I understand they will be any day.
I hope the minister will consider some of my proposals and, in co-operation with other departments, will do some long term planning to solve the problems facing the fishermen. We are not asking that everything be done this year, but we would like to know the plans for next year.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to congratulate the minister on his

appointment, and to say that I hope he will last the full four years and that he has no intention of moving to the other place, because his department is a very important one requiring the direction of a senior cabinet minister like himself.
In his opening remarks he mentioned the cooling of inflation tendencies in the construction industry. This is in direct contrast to what the former minister said in his opening remarks last year, when he presented the estimates to the standing committee, upon which occasion he said:
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We expect that this increase in our construction activities for 1967-68 will provide some relief to the construction industry which has been experiencing a decline in its activities.
I should like to point that out to the minister. Here we have a former minister talking about a decline in construction activities while the present minister wants to cool the inflationary tendencies in the construction industry. He also mentioned the improvement in buildings, when putting in more paper. This appears to be the paper generation. I am just wondering if he is the minister amongst the cabinet ministers who wants to be the most Xeroxed. I hope that does not apply to the Minister of Public Works. The minister used the phrase-and it is quite popular these days: This is modular co-ordination. Perhaps he could tell us in more precise terms what he meant by modular co-ordination.
I thought these estimates would have gone to the standing committee on national resources and public works, because of the necessity for a detailed study which would require the officials of the department to give answers to some of the problems that face us. I can recall that when we had those officials before the standing committee last year there was quite an array of them. I notice that tonight there are very few officials in the gallery and it would be nice to know that we could have them available to answer any questions that come up.
The other important aspect is that I thought we could examine the new departmental organization which should be examined on the basis of the functioning of the various branches. As you know, the reorganization was based on the theme of decentralization of authority to 6 regions and 18 districts. The headquarters organization was changed from one based on functions to be performed to one based on the sequence of
November 4, 1968

operations applying to projects. There aie three different branches: one, programs and planning; two, design and, three, construction and operation.
Then, there was to be a program evaluation directorate, as well as three separate directorates which would provide financial, personnel and administrative support services. There was also to be a change in procedures between programs and projects. It would have been very nice to have before the committee the full array of officials who are responsible for these different changes and organizations, to give us their reactions to the changes in organization.
One feels, Mr. Chairman, that the minister must be the leader of this department and not the follower. We have found in the past that many civil servants lead the minister to the point where he is just like a marionette. This particular minister, during his period with Indian Affairs and Northern Development, was a leader. I would hope he would lead this department and not be a marionette at the behest of senior officials.
Last year during the consideration of the estimates we were supplied not only with a chart setting for the reorganization but a pamphlet with regard to tendering procedures. If I read this pamphlet correctly, there is a main principle with regard to tendering which is set forth in government contract regulations. This principle is, in effect, that before any construction contract is entered into the contracting authority shall invite tenders. There are three exceptions set forth. The first is where the contract is for less than $15,000. The second is where the contract is one related to a pressing emergency in which a delay would be injurious to the public interest. The third is that the work can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the employees of the appropriate contracting authority.
Now, you can state the general rule that there must be tenders, with three exceptions. This rule applies to four main types of contracts dealing with public works. There are construction contracts, purchase contracts, service contracts and leases. We find this pamphlet also contains a description of tendering, which reads:
"tender" means,
(i)	with respect to a construction contract, a tender invited by public advertisement, and
(ii)	with respect to a purchase or service contract, a tender invited by public advertisement or from a representative list or representative lists of suppliers.
Supply-Public Works
So, Mr. Chairman, there is the general rule with regard to tendering. It means that with regard to any construction contract treasury approval is necessary unless the contract is less than $15,000. If it is more than $15,000 and not more than $1 million, two tenders are necessary. I should like to ask the minister or his officials just what the breakdown is with regard to the different types of tenders for the different types of contracts. For instance, I should like to know how many construction contracts we had which were between $15,000 and $1 million. How many tenders were made with regard to those contracts? I should like to know also just how many contracts we had over a million dollars where treasury approval was necessary, and just how many tenders we received for them.
The reason for my request, Mr. Chairman, is that I feel the Canadian public have been milked by many contractors on government contracts. The sophistication in contracting firms today is something of which Canadians should be aware. I am advised that some of them have the same ownership but different names. For instance, in the province of Ontario we have about six major contractors, and even though the names are different the ownership is the same. When a tender is given on a government contract, in truth and in fact one and the same contractor is bidding on the job. It does not matter whether you have one, two or five of these particular contractors because, in reality, you have the same owner. They agree amongst themselves who will take the particular government job. Having agreed, the bids are then presented and are slanted to the position where the one that is selected obtains the job. If this is so, I would think the only way to look into the matter would be to get the owners of these different contracting firms before a committee, and make a thorough study of the ownership situation. As I say, the ownership is very sophisticated and is difficult to determine.
As an example, let me cite the Mannix Construction Company in the west. Mannix Construction was a privately owned contracting firm but was sold to a particular group of contractors. Mr. Mannix remained as president, so you can see that the public would believe he was still the owner of the firm. But he is not the true owner. These are some of the things that we, as a committee, should be studying. If we are overpaying on contracts, then we should know to whom we are overpaying. We should know who are the true owners of these contracting firms, because

November 4, 19G8
Supply-Public Works these firms do make contributions to political parties. If this is so, then we should know who is making the contribution. The least the government could do is to have some type of clause in their contracts prohibiting the firm involved from making a contribution to any political party.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
These are some of the matters on which I should like the minister to dwell when he deals with tendering on some of the contracts let by the government. This particular department, Mr. Chairman, is going to spend $306 million, which is an increase over last year's $294 million. That is a lot of money and I think we should have full value for it. We should also have answers to our questions.
I should now like to direct my mind to the third aspect of the operations of the minister's department, namely the question of waterfront lots. I am sure the minister remembers the heated debates that took place last session on the subject of waterfront lots in the Toronto area, more especially those in which the former member for York-Humber engaged. During those debates the hon. member obtained a legal opinion from the former minister of public works, and I should just like to make reference to the former minister's remarks on the subject of this legal opinion as they are reported at page 3367 of Hansard for March 29, 1966, where he said:
Mr. Chairman, last Friday when these estimates were being discussed some questions were raised about the problem created by the practice ol fill being put in waterlots along a long stretch of the shore of lake Ontario. The same matter was raised again today. I think I should explain where the responsibility of this parliament lies and how the situation is somewhat complicated by a division of jurisdiction.
Now comes the legal opinion, Mr. Chairman.
The provinces own the land under the water, in other words, these waterlots, and it can be transferred by them to private owners, as is the case in the situation presently under discussion. When private owners acquire the waterlots the federal government cannot interfere with that in any way. Then the municipal affairs department of the province and the governments of the municipalities have jurisdiction in the ordinary way over building permits and that sort of thing. The federal authority has jurisdiction over the subject of navigation, and it is only in that connection that it is able to have any legislative responsibility and can take legislative action as set out in the Navigable Waters Protection Act. The difficulty in this particular case-and I am very quick to admit it is a real difficulty-is that of a person owning the lot getting a building permit from the municipality in the usual way.

So from the former minister of public works, Mr. Chairman, you get the legal opinion that this waterfront property is owned by the province, but that there is a divided jurisdiction between the federal authority and the provincial authority.
You might ask, Mr. Chairman, just why I am inquiring about this matter. I should like to ask the minister as to the position of the federal government in regard to the Roberts Bank property in British Columbia. If the position is that the province owns the land under the water, then all that the provincial premier has to do is to convey it to the proper authority, and then the proper authority has full control and jurisdiction over the property. The present minister has taken a very active part in the Roberts Bank dispute and has said that the federal authority has full responsibility. If we were to apply the legal opinion and the reasoning used by the former minister of works, then we may find, Mr. Chairman, that it is the province that has full authority. We are going to spend a great deal of money on the Roberts Bank project, Mr. Chairman, so I think we should clear up once and for all who it is has authority over the waterfront lot on which the harbour is going to be built. We would not want to invest so much money unless we had full control over the property.
The last item I should like to discuss is the co-ordination of his department with others. What co-ordination exists between the minister's department and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. If ever a problem was plaguing Canadians these days, it is that of pollution. I think the Department of Public Works should work hand in hand with whatever department of the federal government has responsibility for that problem. I should like a statement from the minister concerning the co-ordination that is necessary to solve this problem. Mr. Chairman, while we are dealing with the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I would blame myself if I did not point out to the minister how essential it is not to spend all his budget in some ridings which seem favoured by the government, at the expense of other ridings.
For instance, in my own riding, for a long time we have been asking for repairs to the post-office or for a new building, and it is precisely the Department of Public Works which should look after that. A few years ago, the old post office is Rouyn was repaired and an annex was added which, strangely enough, looks a lot like any hen-house we can see many in various parts of the country. A hen-house which is called the post office, right in the middle of the town of Rouyn, is certainly not very aesthetic.
When I mentioned the fact to the minister-not this minister but the previous Conservative minister-everyone wondered what had happened. Did the government architects lack judgment or did the government not know who to hire as a qualified architect to draw the plans so that our post office would look like one.
We still have that post office in the city of Rouyn which is in the last analysis the metropolis of northwestern Quebec. Beautiful post offices were built in Noranda, Val-d'Or, Malartic. But in Rouyn, it seemed good enough to build an addition to the existing post office dating back to 1928, I think, and it is a sorry sight as far as public buildings are concerned.
Many requests have been made over the years to the present Minister of Public Works and to his predecessors. For instance, there is in Notre-Dame-du-Nord an old bridge which must date back to the time when the Oblate Fathers were living in the old fort at Ville-Marie and there were only vehicles drawn by animals. In those days two ox-drawn carts could meet on that bridge but today, it would be nice if two cars could do the same, but it is rather difficult. Quite often, one car has to wait until the other has crossed the bridge, which is rather a long one. Such a state of affairs in 1968, in a region like Temis-camingue, does not make drivers very happy. Even if those who use horses or oxen today can quite easily cross that bridge, cars and
I am told that the department is trying to negotiate the sale of that bridge to the provincial authorities. I cannot recall for how many years there has been talk of that alleged intention of selling the bridge at Notre-Dame-du-Nord to the provincial authorities, but it belongs to the federal government at the present time. We have been waiting to hear about it for a long time. I understand that the budgets are not generous enough to allow the Minister of Public Works to authorize such constructions at the present time, but a start must be made. People have been asking for a new bridge at Notre-Dame-du-Nord for over 10, 15 or 20 years and the money has never been found to build one. Even when the riding was represented by a Liberal member, under a Liberal government, or by a Conservative member, under a Conservative Government, no way was found to improve that situation.
There is another problem, which is serious enough for the farmers of Temiscamingue: Lake Temiscamingue, one of the most beautiful lakes in Canada, is eroding its shores. For years now the government has been asked to build retaining walls to keep the waters from eroding the land of farmers who have been settled along the shores for several years. There again, we are told that the budget does not allow it. Still, during the election campaign, some time in May, a Mr. Bedard, a civil servant of the Department of Public Works, went over to grant small contracts in the riding of Temiscamingue to repair the wharves or, for instance, to put up $125 or $150's worth of rubber along a ramp. If he refuses, tell him to call me. When the man told the bank manager to

Now, with respect to the Department of Public Works, I have nothing else to say this evening, because I do not want to delay the consideration of the estimates. Now, Mr. Chairman, I ask the minister to consider the possibility of acceding to my requests for the constituency of Temis-camingue. Since other members are making

In my riding of Cochrane is the town of Kapuskasing in which is a landmark known for many years as the Kapuskasing Inn. This is a solid brick and steel building worth about $750,000. It was erected some years ago by the Spruce Falls Power and Paper Company and was used as a hotel until recently. A few weeks ago the building was closed because it represented a liability; the company is not in the hotel business. I happen to know that the company in question would be interested in making this building available for community use, provided some

good use would be served by it. The provincial government has looked into this, and is still considering it.
I have asked two departments of government whether they would be interested in this building. I asked the Department of Manpower and Immigration whether the building might not be used as a training school for the forest industry-the most important industry in our region. I have had occasion to talk to these gentlemen, and I may say that I hope the kind of attitude I found prevalent in talking to them is also the attitude of the new minister. I am sure it is. I hope the minister will enhance the very good relations we already have.
The estimates of this department, of course, are always of great interest to parts of Canada such as the Atlantic region because, as my colleague pointed out a minute ago, this is one area where the taxpayer gets little return from his heavy taxation. Quite a change is taking place in the various departments in areas such as regional development, fisheries, post offices, and so on. I am aware that many of these programs, which will be co-ordinated by the Minister of Public Works, must be co-ordinated in co-operation with the various other government departments. We would not like to see tabled in the interim the projects which we hope will materialize in the Atlantic region, before the necessary formal restructuring takes place.
Sometimes governments are apt to become so taken up in the restructuring or setting up of the framework of departments that they forget to govern at all. I hope this will not be an accusation which can be made about this department. I have noticed with some dismay the reductions in the expenditures under the Department of Public Works specifically as they relate to the province of Newfoundland. I notice too with a little reservation the minister's statement about the cooling off of inflationary tendencies. This has already been mentioned by a number of hon. members. I have one great reservation in this regard, because it seems to me rather contradictory to be talking about regional development on the one hand, thereby suggesting some special arrangement and programs, while on the other hand talking about the curtailement of the operational programs and expendiures.
The minister who is responsible for regional development made a statement to the Atlantic provinces economic council last week in which he referred to the great problems the government has in coming to grips with the necessity for stimulating regional development. On the one hand there is a problem in respect of stimulation of growth, while on the other hand there is apparently a need to cool off inflationary tendencies in areas such as central Canada.
There is a great challenge in this regard because any government program which is adopted on a national basis without regard for regional programs will have an adverse effect on areas such as the Atlantic region. The minister responsible for regional development is quite aware of this. I am sure the Minister of Public Works is equally aware of the fact that we cannot accept national policies and a curtailment of programs and expenditures at the risk of a lack of regional development.
The minister of regional development mentioned that there is difficulty in trying to curtail inflationary tendencies in Canada, while at the same time providing employment for the Atlantic region. Surely this necessitates a broadening of programs and government expenditure. This is one of the great contradictions in the various operations of government departments.
I have noticed in the last two weeks that almost every statement emanating from the government benches has had reference to curtailment and balanced budgets. They have
Supply-Public Works referred to cutting down on expenditures. The estimates we have before us now indicate a cut in expenditures in one small area by almost one half. This is contradictory to the philosophy of the present government that it will provide for regional development.

Let me express one grave reservation I have about one particular thing that has been brought to the attention of the minister's department. I represent the great town of Gander, Newfoundland, where the international airport is situated. This is one of the finest towns in the whole of Canada, and if it

I was hoping that this would not come to pass. In the past few years this has been one of the busiest small towns in Canada. Right now we have a very inadequate public building. What this new plan will provide is modest post office facilities and accommodation for various government department officials in various new offices throughout the town. This is certainly not the way to achieve some of those ends indicated by the minister in his preliminary statement.

hope he will at least give consideration to investigating this situation and, like the Minister of Transport, I hope he will heed the advice of the people from these areas, because they know all too well the problems facing these communities. I say to the minister that we do need this building and I assume he will take note of what I am saying and have his officials investigate the matter and remedy these present inadequate public facilities in the town of Gander.
I could go on for quite some time outlining a number of problems, but there are other hon. members who have problems of equal importance.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I hope we can all accomplish as much as we did this afternoon in the debate on the estimates of the department of supply and services. There was such a spirit of camaraderie prevalent this afternoon and there were so many bouquets flying around that one might have thought the government and the opposition had declared a truce.
In the short time allotted I wish only to make one plea, and my request deals with the harbour development in the city of Corner Brook, Newfoundland. I cannot stress enough the vital importance to the future economy of the whole of western Newfoundland of the completion of this project. The port of Corner Brook serves the city of some 30,000 people and it is rapidly becoming the main distributing centre of goods and supplies for western and northwestern Newfoundland and Labrador, an area with a population of over 130,000 people.
The development of new roads and bridges has made this port an essential transportation link and the gateway to the whole new and exciting area of Newfoundland. The central section of the existing Corner Brook waterfront consists of docks of Bowater and Western Terminals and the C.N.R. wharf. These docks which were built on timber piles in 1920 and should have collapsed years ago are inadequate for the volume of cargo passing through them. It was predicted that these wharves would not last beyond 1967. However, at great expense they were planked and stitched together last year, and are in such bad shape that the main carriers threaten they will abandon their service after this season. Trucking concerns will not let their heavy trucks over the wharves for fear of collapse. Last year Western Terminals handled over 74,000 tons of cargo. This could
November 4, 1968

have been much more but for the danger of landing cargoes in excess of the minimum tonnage.
The payroll of the casual workers is around a half million dollars, and some 200 workers are employed. Representations have been made mainly by the chamber of commerce of Corner Brook since 1964 to all levels of government, outlining the critical condition of the wharves and the effect on the economy of the city, and indeed of the whole western part of Newfoundland.
It is noted in the estimate that only $200,000 is allocated toward the provision of new wharving and dock facilities for 1968-1969. However, this money is provided, as I understand, from the Public Works Department for pile testing, designs and other preliminary work. It follows therefore that with this amount of money it will not be possible to start construction in the same year. If this construction is not started next year I should like to point out to the minister that some 200 men will be put out of work and some half million dollars will be lost in pay to these employees. Further, the loss of this service will have far reaching effects on the provision of goods and services to the whole of the great northern peninsula.
If the minister responsible for regional development is sincere in this planned outline for all parts of the Atlantic region, and since the Minister of Public Works will no doubt be working closely with that department, I urge him to heed my request, which is offered with sincerity, to adopt emergency measures so that moneys will be provided to complete the harbour development project in Corner Brook and to save the government serious repercussions which would otherwise arise if this project is not completed next year.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister for some information on several points. Coming from the Vancouver area I wonder what projects are planned to replace those that would have been possible with the winter works program. I have in mind the fact that unemployment figures were very much higher last winter in the months of November and December than they had been in the previous year in those two months, and that there is every indication that they will be going up higher again in these same two months. I wonder what program the minister is planning to supply as an alternative program to the winter works, because I am sure it will be necessary.
Supply-Public Works
He will remember that before we came here at the beginning of this year we attended a meeting of a number of workers from various trades in the North Vancouver shipyards in connection with shipbuilding, construction work and manufacturing. We were impressed by the large percentage of people who were laid off when the winter months came on. I have been looking at the estimates of the department and I just cannot find any project which I believe would be sufficient to care for the number of unemployed people there will be in this winter period.
The second point to which I should like to refer briefly relates to Roberts Bank. My colleague, the hon. member for Broadview, spoke about the recent opinion given by the former minister of public works, that the land comprised by the waterlots is within provincial jurisdiction. I am wondering how this will apply to the harbour and other attendant facilities at Roberts Bank. In other words, I wonder if the minister could let us know how the jurisdiction will be divided between the provincial and federal governments in connection with Roberts Bank, what facilities the federal government intends to build there and what will be left to the province-or perhaps I should say, what the province will leave to the federal government. It seems to me that we would be doing very well if we could get the legal opinion which the Minister of Transport assured us was being sought as to jurisdiction in the matter of Roberts Bank. I should like to ask the minister to enlighten the house as to the jurisdiction of his department in connection with the harbour facilities.
When I was on the west coast recently I heard that the provincial government was planning to take upon itself the building of quite a number of the facilities and that it might even lease them out to foreign companies. I would certainly like to hear what the minister has to say with regard to harbour facilities at Roberts Bank.
There is another matter I would like to bring up. Early this year I received letters from the building service employees union on the coast in connection with a cleaning contract they had with the Vancouver post office. They were complaining that the federal government did not adopt the policy of awarding contracts only to union firms, that it insisted on pursuing the policy of letting contracts to the lowest bidder without any particular concern for what it meant in terms of working conditions for the workers involved.

November 4, 1968
Supply-Public Works
I took this up with the then minister of public works and he told me that this had indeed been the policy, that it was not necessarily union firms which received these cleaning contracts. I would like to impress upon the minister that in awarding contracts to cleaning and other firms a policy should be adopted of dealing strictly with union firms, because it seems to me to be improper for the federal government to set such a poor example of dealing with non-union firms in awarding these contracts.
There are a number of other matters that I would like to raise but I think I had better confine myself to these three specific points. The first question is, what are the major works planned by the minister as a substitute for the winter works program which will be adequate to handle this problem, one which is always complicated in the sea of unemployment.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The second matter is Roberts Bank. How is the division of facilities going to be made between the federal and provincial authorities and what facilities has the federal government clear authority to build? The third question is this: Will the government consider revising its policy to one of dealing strictly with union firms in awarding cleaning and other contracts in public buildings?

I listened with interest to the minister's statement, Mr. Chairman. I was rather intrigued by his suggestion that members of parliament could refer their requests for various constituency public works projects to the regional head offices. Perhaps he may be able to report on this, because in our particular case I understand that the Newfoundland regional head office is located in Halifax. In many instances I would suggest- and certainly it has been our experience in other areas when we have regional head offices located in the maritime provinces- that they are not fully conversant with the peculiar problems of the province of Newfoundland. I understand that perhaps the minister was referring to what could be considered miscellaneous public works, that is works under a value of $50,000.
I share with other hon. members a certain amount of disappointment over the fact that the estimates have not been referred to the committee. There are a number of questions of a detailed nature which we would like to direct to the officials of the department, and naturally many of us are reluctant to take up

the time of the committee with probing questions of a detailed nature. The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate referred to the vote under harbours, rivers and engineering services and compared that to the vote last year for Newfoundland. He referred to the substantial reduction. I should like to hear the minister comment on this reduction, because I think our problems in this particular area of public works, which is so important to Newfoundland, far from diminishing are increasing yearly. If anything, we would have expected the estimates under this particular vote, which as I have said is so important to Newfoundland, would have increased substantially. It is interesting to note the comparison of this vote under harbours, rivers and engineering services with the New Brunswick vote.
Even though it, too, has been reduced as compared with last year, nevertheless it is still in excess of the vote for Newfoundland. I do not feel it is unfair of me to point out that in Newfoundland our problems are much more substantial, much more numerous. We have many more harbours, many more marine facilities because of the vast coastline of the province of Newfoundland, taking in as it does the coast of Labrador.
In connection with these estimates, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer briefly to the St. John's harbour development. I note that the vote for this year for St. John's harbour is merely $100,000. I should like to know, for example, what this covers because we have been hearing now for a number of years suggestions that the Department of Public Works of the government of Canada would be extending the St. John's harbour development to include the eastern end of the harbour. Since some of the harbour development has been completed, there has been a quite unexpected increase in the amount of traffic flowing into the harbour of St. John's. Obviously, this is a direct result of the improved facilities that we now have in that very important port. For example, I should like the minister to tell us if there are plans to proceed with the extension of St. John's harbour. We had hoped there would be some word in this particular direction this year because, as I say, the need is great and is growing steadily.
In so far as accommodation is concerned, I should like to endorse the comments of the hon. member for Cochrane. I, too, am of the opinion that members of parliament, in constituencies where there are public buildings,.
November 4, 1968
should be provided with accommodation so they can properly discharge their duties while the House of Commons is not sitting, or indeed while it is sitting. There are many occasions upon which we have to go to our constituencies to attend to constituency public business. Many of us are at a disadvantage because we have no place from which to operate. We have no place in which to receive our constituents, no place in which to correlate our activities in relation to our responsibilities as members of parliament.
In the general area of accommodation, there is an acute shortage in the city of St. John's. I do not believe anyone will quarrel with that statement. We are experiencing overcrowding in our various government of Canada buildings. Many of our departments are housed in temporary quarters which were acquired as a result of the United States vacating military establishment in St. John's. These temporary accommodations are inadequate to serve the needs and various important functions of the federal government.
I feel it is about time the government of Canada gave serious consideration to the construction of a new public building to house these various departments that are now in temporary quarters. This would alleviate the acute overcrowding that exists in the main public building which is now most inadequate to the needs of the government in my province. There is one other important question which I should like to have answered, because I am a little confused about the relationship between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Fisheries. Many of us who come from the maritime areas are continually made aware of this problem.
For example, we go to the Department of Public Works to request a new, modern facility for a small fishing activity in a particular area. The Department of Public Works will tell us this matter has to be referred to the Department of Fisheries. We go to the Department of Fisheries and we are told by the Department of Fisheries that they cannot justify this expenditure because there is not sufficient fishing activity being conducted in that particular area. It evolves down to the old question, then, of which comes first, the chicken or the egg.
